state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of your previous misconceptions. Just like how changing the units or the average didn't affect the range, changing the heights of the plants by cutting them in half or growing them by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) should also affect the range. So, who do you think is correct now?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get it a bit better now. So, if I cut all the plants in half, the range would still change, right? And if I add \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each plant, that would change the range too? But why does changing the numbers like that affect the range?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it this way: changing the heights of the plants is like adjusting the parts of a ratio. Just like how changing one part in a ratio doesn't mean the quantities will differ by one unit, changing the heights of the plants will result in a different range. So, changing all the heights by the same proportion will definitely affect the range.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming cutting in half affects range when it doesn't, and using confusing ratio analogies), fails to engage the actual misconception meaningfully, and the student becomes more confused rather than developing correct understanding.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use analogies (units, ratios), these are abstract mathematical concepts rather than concrete real-world everyday situations, and the explanations actually contain mathematical errors that confuse rather than ground the concept experientially.
